summary: A 1970 note on interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network, by D. C. Walden. It discusses how programs on different computers might talk to each other. It was replaced by RFC 62.

eli5.summary: This note explores how programs on different computers could talk to each other. A newer note replaced it.

subtitle: A 1970 design for how separate computers in a network could communicate.

tldr.problem: In the early ARPA network, there was no standard system for programs on different computers to communicate with each other and share resources.
tldr.mechanism: This 1970 document proposes a model based on interprocess communication primitives (ports, messages, SEND/RECEIVE operations, and a rendezvous system) that can work both within a single time-sharing system and across a distributed network through a Network Controller.
tldr.outcome: The design influenced the development of the ARPA network protocol suite, but was superseded by RFC 62, which refined the concepts further.

today: RFC 61 is historic and obsoleted by RFC 62, which refined these concepts further. It offers a window into early thinking about network protocol design and influenced the development of the ARPA network's upper-layer protocols.

sections.title: The Challenge of Network Resource Sharing
sections.content: This 1970 note by Dave Walden of BBN addresses the problem of interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network. A resource-sharing network is one where programs on one computer can use the resources (files, processors, memory) of other computers. Walden argues that the fundamental problem is how to allow a process (a running program) on one machine to communicate reliably with a process on another. He develops a model based on the capabilities of time-sharing operating systems of that era.
sections.eli5: When different computers are connected, their programs need to talk to each other. This note figures out how to make that work using ideas from how programs talk within a single computer.

sections.title: Ports and Messages
sections.content: Walden's model centers on ports, which are numbered data channels to or from a process. Two processes communicate by executing matching operations: one executes a RECEIVE at a port, the other executes a SEND to that port. The monitor (operating system) matches them up and transfers the message. A process can also execute RECEIVE ANY to accept messages from any sender, or SEND FROM ANY to broadcast. Each SEND or RECEIVE has four parameters: source port, destination port, a buffer specification, and a target location where the process resumes after transmission.
sections.eli5: Programs get numbered mailboxes (ports). One program puts a letter in a mailbox, another picks it up. The operating system makes sure they match up correctly.

sections.title: Extending to a Network
sections.content: To scale across a network, the SEND and RECEIVE operations are modified to specify a rendezvous site—the location where two processes will meet. When a process at site K sends to site L, the rendezvous normally happens at site L. A RECEIVE message is transmitted to the rendezvous site and placed in a table; when a matching SEND arrives, they are paired up and the data flows back to the source. The RFC includes detailed examples with diagrams showing how two processes at different sites can establish communication through this rendezvous mechanism, and how ports can be passed between processes to enable long-lived connections.
sections.eli5: When sending across a network, two computers pick a meeting place (rendezvous site) where they promise to match up their SEND and RECEIVE messages. This way, each computer knows where to look for the other.
